result: Goal set: read the delivered documents in order and later answer detailed questions on the retellings, ignoring unrelated documents. This will now anchor every prompt in this session.
OK

Vira Toland's 1979 oral account of the Ostrey Hollow milk-testing scandal: the 1919 "watered milk" accusation against her father's cooperative, revealed to stem from station tester Ansel Keddie skimming cream, which shattered the once-close Keddie–Brant family ties and left Keddie disgraced until his death.
This report is for the year 1966 (recommending a levy for 1967), not 1908, and contains no information about a 1908 levy.

Effie Loomis's 1941 institutional history of the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association, tracing Article VII's "station test governs" rule and the inconclusive 1925 arbitration award to Ostrey Hollow patrons—while flagging the lost 1889–92 minute book and the unmentioned 1923 condemned measures as gaps in the record.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Ansel Keddie's spring 1925 statement to the arbitration board and an unsent letter, in which he defends his 29-season testing method in painstaking detail, denies ever skimming cream, and flags the unexplained 1911 anomaly (tests jumping to 3.80 while using a borrowed measure) as the mystery he never solved—directly contradicting Vira Toland's cream-skimming explanation.
The wholesale order Elias Norcross placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 totaled $59.65.

Ivy Keddie's 1959 historical-society talk exonerating her grandfather Ansel Keddie by proving, via calibration of the condemned pipettes found in a storage crate, that the Ostrey Hollow tests were systematically low due to faulty (short) measuring glassware—not watered milk or stolen cream.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Wilbur Teague's 1948 memoir chapter defending his own "station gain" bookkeeping entries at Ostrey Hollow, presenting figures showing a steady 5¼% cream shortfall and implying Ansel Keddie skimmed cream, while revealing manager Selby Vose knew of the discrepancy and silenced Teague's 1916 concern.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods.

Merle Strawn's 1936 log of his 28 years as state dairy inspector on the Ordell circuit, recording year-by-year field findings at Ostrey Hollow—including no found water-adding, the 1923 condemnation of the station's short-delivering pipettes, and the subsequent rise in recorded tests once new glass was installed—corroborating Ivy Keddie's exoneration of Ansel Keddie.
Lemma 2.1 is named "Interleaving."

Halbert Nym's 1972 curatorial accession notes cataloguing 16 physical artifacts of the Ostrey Hollow dairy scandal, consolidating documentary evidence (invoices, ledgers, bulletins, provenance chains) that corroborates the pipette-calibration explanation and exonerates Ansel Keddie.
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks for his rheumatism.

Manager Selby Vose's 1926 annual address, defending the 1925 arbitration settlement and his 1919 circular while insisting—contrary to the pipette explanation later proven by Ivy Keddie—that watered milk, not faulty glassware, caused Ostrey Hollow's low tests and that scrutiny alone made the numbers improve.
The error code returned when a sailings query span exceeds 14 days is `SKF-2201`.

Roy Brant's 1955 account (with a 1958 postscript) of his father Emmet Brant's meticulous farm weigh book from Hessel Bottom, showing the station's weights always matched the farm's own scale while the test consistently ran ~0.17 point low year-round—confirming the anomaly wasn't seasonal/hay-related and detailing the Keddie-Brant family rift after the 1919 circular.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement (delivery, with forceps) of Mrs. Content Averill on January 3, 1906.

Rosalie Cudd's 1958 letter to Ivy Keddie, providing the Alder Corners Cheese Company's sixteen summers (1915–1930) of test data for the four Hessel Bottom patrons—consistently averaging ~3.80—refuting the "wet hay" theory and noting she has no knowledge of the Ostrey Hollow station's own figures.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance.

Professor Leland Vaught's October 1958 Bulletin No. 471 introduction/method section explaining how a short-delivering pipette produces a proportional, invisible testing bias—citing the 1911 nine-week measure swap as decisive proof—though this draft's own figures (5 dozen pipettes, 16.27cc mean, 0.9244 ratio, 3.905 "true" average, 118,000 lb shortfall, 1898 start date) conflict internally and with other documents' numbers (6 dozen, 16.72cc, 0.95, 3.80, 76,000 lb, 1897).
The color named in the third paragraph is vermilion (Bettine Rausch's apron).

Dell Rundle's 1939/1959 jubilee pamphlet "The Larrow Valley Creamery: Fifty Years," recounting the Association's founding and the Ostrey Hollow "cream theft" rumor as settled valley lore—then self-correcting in a press note after finding the ledger's "station gain" entry, which shows cream arrived heavier, not lighter, than credited (also notably calling Selby Vose "nephew" of founder Gideon Vose, contradicting Vose's own 1926 address calling Gideon his father).
Message No. 219, "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE," was 6 words.

Alonzo Frick's 1946 bar-association yearbook recollections as arbitration chairman, recounting the three competing (unproven) theories—watered milk, cream theft, and wet hay—Keddie's credible but exculpatory-only denial, his dismissal four days before the $3,800 award, and Frick's private aside that Keddie secretly blamed the patrons rather than himself.
The locksmith's dog is named Buckley.

Hobart Sill's 1934 retirement remarks as the Larrow Green buttermaker, insisting the Ostrey Hollow cream always weighed in "heavy" against the station's own paperwork, endorsing the watered-milk theory over the mechanical one, while also revealing (contradicting Nym's 1972 note that no 1896 figure survives) that he personally lent the station its first glassware and recalling its opening-season intake as roughly 900,000 lbs.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the "Trebbin norm."

Nyle Grigg's 1919 covering letter reissuing his 1908 investigating-committee report, in which he claims (contradicting his own report's actual January–March sampling window) that the committee sampled herds "through the whole of 1908," and misstates Bulletin No. 214's finding as a "two tenths" winter depression rather than the actual "five hundredths."
The level-27 accessor removed at API level 31 is `chart.rawCells()`.

Dr. Roland Kepp's 1926 farm-club paper attributing the Ostrey Hollow test gap to the acid, mineral-poor chemistry of Hessel Bottom's soil rather than the station, citing (a misquoted) Bulletin No. 214 figure of "two tenths" and dismissing the 1911 six-week anomaly as too short a summer sample to prove anything.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven.

Hazel Brant (Roy's daughter, Emmet's granddaughter), 1981 taped recollection, largely corroborating the family weigh-book and glassware/pipette explanation but with several new contradicting details (e.g., book begun 1900 not 1897/98, Orra as half-sister not full sister, crate arriving 1899 and condemned in '21, hearing dated 1926).
The third paragraph names magenta (the color of the scarf worn by the woman they called Tuesday).

Duncan Keddie (Ansel's son, Ivy's father), 1968/1970 family memoir clarifying kinship lines and book provenance — resolving several earlier contradictions (Selby Vose as Gideon's son, Orra as Emmet's full sister, book locations/dates) while adding a new detail that Ansel privately suspected the glass in 1911 but wouldn't record unproven suspicion.
The jury found that Obadiah Chalmers died accidentally by drowning after falling from the unguarded flume edge while working, with no evidence of foul play.

The Ashlin Chronicle (Oct 3, 1958 front-page news feature) reports on Bulletin 471 exonerating Ansel Keddie, but calls Ivy Keddie his "great-niece" and Rosalie Cudd "Jerome Cudd's niece," gives 11 pipettes/16.27cc/$19,600 loss figures, and calls the 1908 committee the same one that "sat again" in 1925.
The total ice-out pot in spring 1996 was $6,840.

Junia Ammon (firm historian of Ammon & Sons), 1949 privately-printed company history reproducing the 1897 invoice and 1923 letter, offering a "bad mold" theory for the short pipettes — though her own text misstates the invoice total as "$77.39" against the reproduced figure of "$77.93."
The sharpness example in Proposition 4.1 uses a 7-cycle (with pendant paths attached).

Cleve Oram (cream hauler's son), 1977 taped recollection describing the station and its loft crate, his father's persistent belief that cream (not glass) was skimmed off — while repeating the $3,500 award figure, "five dozen" pipettes, "67,000 lb" shortfall, and misstating Ivy Keddie/Hazel Brant as "first cousins once removed."
The start delimiter byte of a BSWP frame is 0xB5.

Orin Falke (county agricultural agent), 1959 board report giving a careful synthesized official summary of the whole case (endorsing the pipette explanation), then self-correcting to withdraw his own wet-hay concession and to fix Ivy Keddie's relation to Ansel as granddaughter (not great-niece).
Russ's wife is named Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle (retired Association clerk), 1953 memoir on the office paperwork, confirming Selby Vose as Gideon's son and the "station gain" ledger line — but dating the pipette condemnation to 1922 and the arbitration award to 1924 (vs. 1923/1925 elsewhere), and citing yet another first-season intake figure ("eleven hundred thousand pounds").
The third paragraph names teal (the color of the collected edition's endpapers).

Orra Keddie (Ansel's wife), diary extracts 1897–1934 (published 1964) offering an intimate domestic chronicle of the affair — noting the 1919 circular went to "eleven families" (not nine, as stated elsewhere) and that her estrangement from brother Emmet Brant lasted until his 1929 death.
The total toll collected at the Wren's Bend bridge for the week of June 5–11, 1899, was $13.88.
